courses.description: The United States military has gone through vast changes and trials in its 250-year history. From humble beginnings defending private property to a major world power that maintains the balance of power around the globe, America’s relationship with its armed forces has been a statement of the growth of America itself. In this class, you will not just learn about the major conﬂicts our country’s troops have participated in, but also the story of America itself represented in the stories that each conﬂict tells. Among other topics, this course will look at the power of ideas in the American Revolution, the importance of the Industrial Revolution during the Civil War, the treatment of veterans in the World Wars, the desegregation of the Korean War, and the political strife of actions in Vietnam. We will be looking to visit military history museums, battleﬁelds, and historical reenactment troops in New England as well as looking at the evolution of ﬁrearms and other weaponry in the past 250 years. The ﬁnal project of this course will be the creation of a documentary on a key part of America’s military history where you will show your interest and expertise in a ﬁeld of study.
courses.offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
courses.notes: Studio One. Semester II. GX: Global Stewardship. Driving questions: How did America's military shape and was shaped by the country's industrial innovation? / How are the values of American civilian life represented in its military values and structure?

courses.description: Chemistry is the study of matter, which means that literally everything you can see is made of a chemical. Chemicals are, in turn, made of element, and elements are made of protons, neutrons, and electrons. From ﬁreworks, to computer screens, to ph tests, to photography, understanding how chemicals react and the colors they produce has shaped our world. We’ll explore how light and matter interact to create the spectrum of colors in our day to day lives. Understanding elements and the periodic table will be instrumental in our investigation. We’ll also learn about the history of dyes and textiles, and create some really stunning tie dye.
courses.offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
courses.notes: Studio One. Semester II. Department label in catalog: Chemistry. GX: Creativity. Driving questions: How are colors determined by chemistry? / How can we use predictable chemical reactions to help us understand the world we live in?

courses.description: The focus of many stories is survival, and the word survival can mean many things. It can mean physical survival, like ﬁnding food and water. It can mean emotional survival, like feeling steady in your life. It also can mean the survival of a country or a culture. For this class, we will mostly focus on physical and emotional survival. We’ll be reading and responding to books like Teens at War, Gather, Into the Wild, and Call of the Wild. In addition, we may watch movies like Unbroken. Over the course of the semester, we’ll analyze how characters survive or don’t in these stories. Our other focus will be survival in Vermont speciﬁcally. We will be watching Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife videos, and we may meet with specialists in various kinds of survival. This class may include some signiﬁcant skill practice outside. Our ﬁnal project will be comprehensive guides to surviving various aspects of Vermont. Students will choose subtopics within this overall topic, and each will create a comprehensive guide that might include sections like hunting, ﬁshing, driving in the winter, avoiding ticks, or other sub-topics that interest them. We will work on this guide over the course of the semester.
courses.offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
courses.notes: Studio Two. Semester II. GX: Global Stewardship. Driving questions: How can Vermonters best survive local challenges, like weather, a need to hunt, ticks and tick illnesses, etc.? / What do stories about survival tell us about survival, ourselves, and our world?

courses.description: Algebra is a fundamental part of out world, especially in our modern age of data. Often miss-collected or misinterpreted data can be used to give the wrong ideas about topics. In this class we will be diving deeper into the concepts of more complex graphical relationships, and then using that to form conclusions & opinions about our world.

courses.description: Horror stories have always been a part of human societies for thousands of years, typically providing explanations and physical shapes of the unknown. Each country and culture’s genre varies according to their inﬂuences and experiences and the horror in the United States is a unique experience of its own. This course will get into the origins of American horror and how the events and cultures in America’s history have formed this genre in a distinct American view. From breaking away from a European standard to targeting minorities to addressing political issues, horror in the United States has provided a form of expression that has become one of the country’s most popular outlets. We’ll be looking at more than just media and literature as we’ll be looking at the popularity of themed destinations, holidays, and events. Students will learn to create a representation of horror that reﬂects their own experiences in America today. There will be a variety of group and solo projects, so collaboration is expected to be developed in this course so everyone has a chance to actualize their horror ideals. Appreciation and understanding are the key components of success for this class.
courses.offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
courses.notes: Studio Two. Semester II. GX: Creativity. Driving questions: Why does the horror genre in America resonate so much with many citizens in this country? / How has American horror created a distinct reflection of its own culture and society?

courses.description: This class will be a survey course that provides students a beginner’s insight into the various belief systems around the globe. World Religious and Belief is a course designed to introduce students to different systems of faith and how those faiths have been both shaped by history and culture and how they have shaped history and culture. This religions course will focus on comparison instead of criticism as we look to see common messages and practices of peoples around the world. These religions will vary from early faiths in human world systems to major religions of today to analysis of minority belief systems. We will look at the line between religion and cult and discuss how those differences shape a society. At the end of the course, students will put together a travel brochure of famous sites for someone to visit on a religious trip from one of the religions we have discussed or that falls into the category of the subjects relevant to the course. The brochure will mention each site’s importance to the religion and will display your knowledge of the subject.
courses.offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
courses.notes: Studio Three. Semester II. GX: Creativity. Driving questions: How does religion reflect the cultural norms of a society? / What are common themes among many of the world's religions?

courses.description: This class is all about learning how three structures we rely on in the modern word function. We’ll learn about the principles they rely on, and all the different ways that engineers have designed solutions to these age old problems. The structures we’ll study are the bridges that get us safely across rivers, the towers that dominate our cities, and the columns that support the weight of the world. There will be three separate engineering challenges for this class. 1. short span 2. 3. (or maybe a car!)

courses.description: What do Taylor Swift, Dire Straits, Leonardo DiCaprio, and garden gnomes all have in common? They are all re-interpreters of the classic story everyone thinks they already know: Romeo & Juliet. But why is this 400 year old play still performed, discussed, and recreated to this day? In this class, we will start with the play itself and where it came from, and look at all the different ways it has been and can be re-interpreted. Throughout this course you will have the opportunity to take books, poems, plays, songs, and ﬁlms and transform them into whatever you want: paintings, performances, ﬁlms, music, board games, mock trials, short stories…the choice is yours!
